Brand South Africa

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Brand South Africa spent R8 million a year on their website - was it worth it?

Unique Selling Point:
Exclusive interview with Brand SA's CEO Dr Kingsley Makhubela on why how the organization wastes money and why they are so determined to get rid of him.

Summary:
Digital media agency Avatar were paid R24,6 million over 3 years to design and maintain Brand SA's website. They were also paid an additional R100 000 per month to host the website. When the contract came to an end in 2017, Brand SA issued another tender: this time for 5 years. When Avatar's bid of R45 million with an 80% retainer was rejected, Avatar CEO Zibusiso Mkhwanazi threatened to sue Brand SA CEO Dr Makhubela.

On investigation CEO Makhubela then discovered that Avatar had charged and been R5 million more then they bid in their first contract. When he announced his intention to institute a forensic investigation to the Board Chairman, Khanyisile Kweyama, he himself was the subject of a forensic investigation.

Further information:
Dr Makhubela has been on special leave since April 2018, while the Board and ENS investigated the spurious accusations made against him on the internal Whistleblower Hotline. He has been cleared of all charges, including sexual harassment, yet the Board of Trustees refuses to allow him to resume work.
They have been to the CCMA, yet failed to reach a resolution. He is now calling for arbitration.

Apart from the dodgy Avatar tender and the gross overspend on digital marketing, Dr Makhubela identified other concerns in Brand SA:
1. Senior management received a 25% pay increase every 2 years.
2. The South African employees working in the UK and the USA were paid in US dollars and GB Pounds, contrary to government regulations.
3. The lease of the Brand SA building is exorbitant - over R20 million every 5 years.
4. The Board Chairman wanted to be paid a salary of R800 000 per annum
5. The reputation management company employed by Brand SA is also earning exorbitant fees.

The Auditor-General has identified R10.5 million of irregular expenditure at Brand South Africa.

Press Release:


Divided Brand SA
With the fortunes of South Africa’s state institutions flagging as the President works to attract investment and clean up house through various commissions of inquiry, Carte Blanche examines internal tensions within Brand SA, the custodian of the country’s nation brand. Created in 2002 to foster a positive brand image, rifts have emerged over the awarding of a digital marketing tender. We speak to suspended CEO Kingsley Makhubela and board chairperson Khanyisile Kweyama to ask whether taxpayers are getting value for money from the agency.
Producer: Kate Barry
Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender


Script:


BRAND SA


V/O: At a time when load shedding, the collapse of state institutions like Eskom, and allegations of wholesale corruption and state capture dominate the news, our global image has never needed more work.

These international campaigns have marketed our country ever since the concept of a nation brand was invented. The man who coined the phrase is the founder of the Nation Brand Index, international policy advisor, Simon Anholt.

Simon: The problem is that the phrase “nation brand” got twisted into “nation branding”, because there is absolutely no proof, no evidence whatsoever that communications programs make any difference to the image of a country.

V/O: Brand South Africa has an annual budget of R200 million for reputation management, marketing and communications. The current CEO, Dr Kingsley Makhubela, was head-hunted in 2015.

Kingsley: I was an ambassador in Portugal, an ambassador in Kenya, I was a Chief of State Protocol, I was a deputy Director General at the Department of Foreign Affairs now DIRCO, later on I was a Director General at the Department of Tourism.

V/O: But after mixing with Popes and Presidents, he’s now been suspended for gross misconduct.

Link: Brand SA is the custodian of our national brand, but a recent spate of allegations and counter allegations has left its own reputation ragged at the edges.

V/O: With accusations of sexual misconduct, alleged collusion between staff and contractors and evidence of irregular expenditure, is Brand SA giving South African taxpayers value for money?

In 2014 Brand SA’s digital marketing services were outsourced to A/va/tarr agency. Ava/tarr is owned by successful, young entrepreneurs Zi/busiso Mkhwanazi & Veli Ngu/bane. The contract lasted 3 years, so in 2017 Brand SA issued a new tender.

Kingsley: The team comes to me in 2017, they say to me listen, we have money, we have 45 million. We can run this tender for 5 years.

V/O: They received 21 proposals, and Avatar was the highest scoring bidder. But before the tender could be awarded, the Bid Adjudication Committee picked up a discrepancy in the fees submitted by Ava/tar.

Kingsley: They put in another 10 million over and above the 45 million.

Devi: For what?

Kingsley: They hid them under the tax and hid that under inflation costs. But not only 10 million more: the same tender – people that have taken a decision, have taken the decision outside a committee meeting, that this tender must go to the incumbent company, which is Avatar.

V/O: He cancelled the tender and informed the Board Chair, Khanyi/sile Kwe/yama. This former Director of Anglo American, sits on the board of Telkom and PRASA. She was appointed to Brand SA in 2016.

Kingsley: She said the Avatar guy, came to talk to me, Mkhwanazi, about this, about the cancellation of the tender. And she said to me I told him not to discuss this with me, because it may come to me as a Chair of the Board. I was a bit taken aback that she got involved at that level with a tender.

V/O: We asked the Board Chair about her connection to Mkhwanazi.

Devi: Do you have a relationship with Avatar?

Khanyisile: I don’t have a relationship with Avatar, I know the owner of Avatar, Zibusiso Mkhwanazi. I know him because we are in the same denomination, but we don’t sit in church together every week.

Link: I was looking forward to meeting Zibusiso Mkhwanazi – this new marketing whizz-kid. But strangely enough, he didn’t want to meet me. Instead of an interview he promised to send written answers.

V/O: Despite cancelling the tender, Brand SA needed to keep their 3 websites up and running, so extended Avatar’s contract. They charged a monthly retainer of almost R690 000 plus web hosting fees of almost R100 000. But Avatar had outsourced the web hosting to Hetz/ner. Brand SA now pays Hetzner directly - less than R2500 a month for what appears to be the same package.

Kingsley: R2500 a month, and the conventional wisdom out there is that is actually a lot of money, and they were charging R100 000 for doing nothing.

V/O: But Avatar explained their markup actually included security, technical and maintenance services, not to mention excessive web traffic and server usage. What’s more, the Avatar rates were agreed upon by Brand South Africa.

Text: “…security, technical and maintenance services as part of the hosting fee.”
The amounts differed every single month as it depended on traffic and server usage.
The Avatar rates were agreed upon with BSA based on the approved rate card.




V/O: They re-advertised the R45 million tender, and received 22 bids, including Avatar. But this time an independent expert evaluated the bids, and advised that Avatar’s bid did not meet the 70% minimum score. Yet Brand SA staff seemed determined to re-appoint Avatar.



Kingsley: But what came out of that was shocking because they then went to this expert company, including the head of procurement at Brand SA, to say to the expert company, we want this tender to be given to Avatar. Please, they tried again to change the scoring criteria of how the tender is done.

Devi: So you had your own staff members meddling?

Kingsley: Not meddling, colluding and deciding the tender goes somewhere. As an accounting officer I had the responsibility to report this thing. I reported this to the National Treasurer; I reported to the Auditor General to say this is what’s going on there, because it’s my responsibility as the accounting officer. I can’t conceal corruption. I can’t do that.

V/O: He cancelled it again and decided to re-examine the 2014 tender. Brand SA had asked for a 360-degree digital marketing solution. This covers hosting, security, technical and maintenance services. Avatar bid, and was awarded the contract at R18 million inclusive of VAT. During contract negotiations Avatar amended the agreement to exclude VAT and added a 10% annual increase. Mkhwanazi says he did this because the R18 million should never have included VAT. Brand SA incorporated those changes and the CEO at the time signed on the dotted line. After 3 years Brand SA had paid R22.6 million. The Auditor General has flagged the additional R4.6 million as irregular expenditure.

Devi: We’re talking about R8 million a year for the website. Was it worth it?

Khanyisile: I really don’t have an answer to that. I don’t know enough about website hosting. As a Board that is charged with making sure that taxpayer’s money is spent properly, it does remain a question mark to us.

V/O: But according to the Auditor-General, Brand SA paid Avatar an additional R11 million for ad hoc services not stipulated in the contract. This means a total of R33.7 million on an R18 million rand tender. The Auditor-General says this contravenes the Public Finance Management Act.
Avatar say they didn’t overcharge Brand SA, that the scope changed, and the contract allowed for ad hoc services to be billed separately. Also that the findings of the Auditor-General speak to poor financial controls at Brand SA.


Text: “We did not overcharge Brand SA”

“The scope in the tender is not the same scope in the contract, both provided by Brand SA”

“The findings of the Auditor General are not against Avatar, but Brand SA”

“It speaks to poor financial controls in the way they deal with contracts.”

Kingsley: To tell the truth Devi, we will need to conduct proper forensics to understand the extent and the depth of the rot in Brand South Africa.

V/O: Avatar claims they are caught in the crossfire of an employer/employee dispute, because before Kingsley could commission a proper forensic investigation, Brand SA staff made serious allegations against him.
Text: “This matter is an employer / employee dispute and we are caught in the crossfire.”
Link: Suddenly there was a flurry of complaints on Brand SA’s Whistleblower Hotline. It put a hold on the CEO’s career.

V/O: In April last year he was put on special leave and faced a charge of sexual harassment - a disciplinary hearing found him not guilty. After 11 months at home on full pay, he’s now charged with conflict of interest, for failing to declare his relationship with sGweelie Gumede, the Chairman of the Sport Industry Group.

Devi: How are you related to Mr Gumede?

Kingsley: I’m not even related to him. As I said, he’s married to my ex-wife’s sister.

V/O: Gumede had suggested a collaboration with Brand SA, and Kingsley asked his staff to evaluate it.

Kingsley: I don’t tell them that I know the person, because once I do that the impression will be created that I’m trying to say look at him nicely. They don’t even come back to me.

Devi: I am going to disagree with you on that. I do think you should have made it clear that there was a familiar relationship?.

Kingsley: How do you make it clear to people that you’re saying look if there’s any value for collaboration?

Devi: Then you need to declare what the relationship is?

Kingsley: There’s not even a contract. It’s somebody who says we can do this.

Khanyisile: It’s common anywhere that you must declare. Now in this instance it’s even worse when you refer, then you should say that this is my relative.

Kingsley: Good corporate governance says allow people to give you advice that is not influenced by any idea.

Devi: And good corporate governance also says declare?

Kingsley: Remember you declare once there’s a value; once people say to me there’s a value I would have said listen, I don’t want to get involved in this. Go and have a discussion on this thing because I know the guy.

V/O: After Kingsley’s suspension, Brand SA concluded a R2 million agreement with Gumede which has since been cancelled.

Devi: So why should South Africans care about the shenanigans that have been going on?

Kingsley: These issues are in the interest of the public, we can’t hide it. The public must hold all of us accountable, myself included.

V/O: Germany is currently ranked 1st out of 50 countries on the Anholt Nation Brands Index, while South Africa lags behind in 38th position. But Simon believes it will take more than a marketing campaign to improve our image.

Simon: It’s about how you behave, it’s not what you say about yourself. So, it’s about what you do and about what you’re going to do in the international domain; what you do for humanity and the planet. That’s the only thing, according to the 143 billion data points that I’ve collected through the Nation Brands Index – that’s the only thing that will make a difference to your image.

It put a hold on the CEO’s career. V/O: In April last year he was put on special leave and faced a charge of sexual harassment - a disciplinary hearing found him not guilty. After 11 months at home on full pay, he’s now charged with conflict of interest, for failing to declare his relationship with sGweelie Gumede, the Chairman of the Sport Industry Group. Devi: How are you related to Mr Gumede? Kingsley: I’m not even related to him. As I said, he’s married to my ex-wife’s sister. V/O: Gumede had suggested a collaboration with Brand SA, and Kingsley asked his staff to evaluate it. Kingsley: I don’t tell them that I know the person, because once I do that the impression will be created that I’m trying to say look at him nicely. They don’t even come back to me. Devi: I am going to disagree with you on that. I do think you should have made it clear that there was a familiar relationship?. Kingsley: How do you make it clear to people that you’re saying look if there’s any value for collaboration? Devi: Then you need to declare what the relationship is? Kingsley: There’s not even a contract. It’s somebody who says we can do this. Khanyisile: It’s common anywhere that you must declare. Now in this instance it’s even worse when you refer, then you should say that this is my relative. Kingsley: Good corporate governance says allow people to give you advice that is not influenced by any idea. Devi: And good corporate governance also says declare? Kingsley: Remember you declare once there’s a value; once people say to me there’s a value I would have said listen, I don’t want to get involved in this. Go and have a discussion on this thing because I know the guy. V/O: After Kingsley’s suspension, Brand SA concluded a R2 million agreement with Gumede which has since been cancelled. Devi: So why should South Africans care about the shenanigans that have been going on? Kingsley: These issues are in the interest of the public, we can’t hide it. The public must hold all of us accountable, myself included. V/O: Germany is currently ranked 1st out of 50 countries on the Anholt Nation Brands Index, while South Africa lags behind in 38th position. But Simon believes it will take more than a marketing campaign to improve our image. Simon: It’s about how you behave, it’s not what you say about yourself. So, it’s about what you do and about what you’re going to do in the international domain; what you do for humanity and the planet. That’s the only thing, according to the 143 billion data points that I’ve collected through the Nation Brands Index – that’s the only thing that will make a difference to your image.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Brand South Africa spent R8 million a year on their website - was it worth it?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Exclusive interview with Brand SA's CEO Dr Kingsley Makhubela on why how the organization wastes money and why they are so determined to get rid of him.
metadata.Summary: Digital media agency Avatar were paid R24,6 million over 3 years to design and maintain Brand SA's website. They were also paid an additional R100 000 per month to host the website. When the contract came to an end in 2017, Brand SA issued another tender: this time for 5 years. When Avatar's bid of R45 million with an 80% retainer was rejected, Avatar CEO Zibusiso Mkhwanazi threatened to sue Brand SA CEO Dr Makhubela. On investigation CEO Makhubela then discovered that Avatar had charged and been R5 million more then they bid in their first contract. When he announced his intention to institute a forensic investigation to the Board Chairman, Khanyisile Kweyama, he himself was the subject of a forensic investigation.
metadata.Further information: Dr Makhubela has been on special leave since April 2018, while the Board and ENS investigated the spurious accusations made against him on the internal Whistleblower Hotline. He has been cleared of all charges, including sexual harassment, yet the Board of Trustees refuses to allow him to resume work. They have been to the CCMA, yet failed to reach a resolution. He is now calling for arbitration. Apart from the dodgy Avatar tender and the gross overspend on digital marketing, Dr Makhubela identified other concerns in Brand SA: 1. Senior management received a 25% pay increase every 2 years. 2. The South African employees working in the UK and the USA were paid in US dollars and GB Pounds, contrary to government regulations. 3. The lease of the Brand SA building is exorbitant - over R20 million every 5 years. 4. The Board Chairman wanted to be paid a salary of R800 000 per annum 5. The reputation management company employed by Brand SA is also earning exorbitant fees. The Auditor-General has identified R10.5 million of irregular expenditure at Brand South Africa.
